title: EDUCATION: Challenge Accepted: Jingle-Jangle Fallacies
author: Ben Zulauf
summary: Ben Zulauf introduces two concept-labeling errors that plague educational discourse. The jingle fallacy occurs when the same word is used for different concepts -- the prime example being 'direct instruction,' which simultaneously refers to Engelmann's scripted DI curriculum and the broader pedagogical principles of explicit, systematic instruction (di). The jangle fallacy is the reverse: different words describing the same concept, creating false debates between practitioners who actually agree. When Zulauf surveyed 47 district coaches asking 'what is direct instruction?' he received responses grouping into 10 distinct categories -- empirical proof that shared terminology does not mean shared understanding. He connects these fallacies to the instructional hierarchy (acquisition, fluency, generalization, adaptation), noting that educators at each stage need fundamentally different types of instruction and that mislabeled concepts prevent evidence-based practice from spreading. Terminological clarity is presented as a prerequisite for coherent reform.
points: Jingle fallacy: same word, different concept -- e.g., 'direct instruction' meaning both Engelmann's scripted DI and the broader explicit-instruction principles.
Jangle fallacy: different words, same concept -- creates false debates between practitioners who actually agree.
Survey of 47 district coaches on 'direct instruction' produced 10 distinct definition categories -- empirical proof of the problem's scale.
The instructional hierarchy (acquisition, fluency, generalization, adaptation) requires different instructional approaches at each stage.
Terminological clarity is a prerequisite for spreading evidence-based practice across a school system.
quotes: The jingle fallacy is when the same name is used to describe two different concepts. People are using the same word, but the word has different meanings. The jangle fallacy is when two different words are used to describe the same concept.
DI refers to a very scripted curriculum whereas di is a set of pedagogical principles that can be applied to any curriculum or content.
We were all using the same term -- direct instruction -- but we were definitely not all speaking the same language.
Acquisition -- Learners at this stage are being exposed to a new skill. They benefit from very explicit instruction and feedback so that they can do the skill accurately.
If education in general wants to escape our current jingle fallacy, then we need to know the research.
